title: Renourishing Education’s Soil
author: Kevin Stinehart
summary: Responding to a headline that American schools are sliding toward illiteracy because standards are too low, Kevin Stinehart argues the real problem is depleted developmental soil, not a low bar. He uses a garden metaphor, drawing on Froebel's kindergarten, to claim that pacing guides, benchmark tests and accountability systems reward compliance and speed over depth, and that pulling harder on the stem cannot make anything grow. He reframes student disengagement as a design flaw in learning conditions rather than a character flaw, and redefines rigor as depth rather than pressure. As evidence he offers his own school's Play Club, after which office referrals fell 76 percent and bus referrals 94 percent, and the Finnish redesign of the 1970s. He ends with five steps for rebuilding the conditions of learning, including free play, trusting teachers as designers, and measuring relationships and belonging as indicators of system health.
points: Stinehart inverts the standards-are-too-low narrative: many standards are developmentally too high and have been pushed down into earlier grades.
Disengagement is recast as a signal of poor learning conditions, so blame on grit or lazy teachers is misdirected.
Rigor is redefined as careful cultivation and depth rather than acceleration, with free play and movement named as conditions for executive function and literacy.
Central Academy of the Arts reported a 76 percent drop in office referrals and 94 percent drop in bus referrals after launching Play Club and open before-school play.
The Finland example and the South Carolina graduate profile are offered as proof that systems can be redesigned around child development and teacher agency.
quotes: If anything, many states’ standards are over students’ heads and the rigor is far too fast and intense for most children to have any kind of deep understanding.

Hinnant-Crawford (2020) reminds us that, “Systems produce the outcomes they are designed to produce.” When we design for efficiency instead of understanding, we should not be surprised when learning is shallow and literacy and math skills wane.

We’ve transformed gardens into factories. We mistook rigor for growing deep roots. The structural frame of schooling (schedules, test scores, pacing guides, accountability hierarchies) has eroded the soil of belonging, communication, collaboration, curiosity, and connection that sustains true learning.
Student disengagement often signals a design flaw, not a character flaw. Schools thrive when they help meet children’s basic needs for meaning, belonging, and growth.
We have confused rigor with pressure. True rigor isn’t constant acceleration. It’s careful cultivation. It’s the kind of depth that allows students to explore, question, and thrive.

America’s children aren’t “sliding toward illiteracy” because of our “low standards.” They’re starving for emotional, relational, and social nourishment. Our standards aren’t too low - they’re floating high above parched soil, disconnected from the roots that would sustain them.
